papers.title: Enhancing cortical electrophysiological signatures of sleep overrides ER stress responses in sleep-deprived mice
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation (SD) triggers characteristic changes in the cortical electroencephalogram (EEG) during waking and sleep, as well as upregulating molecular signatures of neuronal activity, synaptic plasticity, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress. This includes the induction of the unfolded protein response (UPR), the primary marker and adaptive mechanism of ER stress. Yet how cortical neuronal activity during SD contributes to the induction of these molecular signatures remains unknown. Here we investigate whether manipulating cortical activity during SD with a physiological stimulation paradigm (flickering light stimulation, FLS) affects the induction of the UPR. As expected, SD alone upregulated activity-dependent and UPR-related genes in cortex and led to increased EEG slow-wave activity (SWA) during subsequent NREM sleep, an electrophysiological signature of sleep need. Delivering FLS during SD, however, prevented the upregulation of activity- and UPR-related genes while inducing an additional increase in SWA during subsequent sleep. Further analysis of neuronal firing revealed that FLS induced brief neuronal silent (OFF) periods in awake animals during stimulation, thereby shifting cortical activity towards a brain state resembling sleep. These findings suggest that physiological manipulation of cortical activity during waking is sufficient to dissociate molecular signatures of ER stress from electrophysiological markers of sleep pressure. We propose that global sleep wake history and cortical network dynamics differentially regulate activity-dependent transcription and the accumulation of sleep pressure.

papers.title: Isoflurane anesthesia CNS recovery state: ultra-slow oscillations and cellular-stress-responsive gene expression
papers.abstract: General anesthesia and NREM sleep share slow-wave EEG features, yet whether anesthesia substitutes for physiological sleep remains unclear. We compared recovery from 4h of isoflurane anesthesia (IA) with time-matched sleep and sleep deprivation (SD) in male C57BL/6J mice using continuous EEG/EMG recordings and frontal cortex RNA sequencing. IA recovery produced transient, rebound arousal, reduced early NREM and REM sleep, and, fragmented subsequent NREM bouts, and persistant, ultra-slow EEG-oscillations that normalized within two weeks. Whereas, SD induced consolidated rebound sleep and slow wave activity. Transcriptomic profiling at ZT6 showed that IA and SD induced largely distinct cortical gene-expression programs. IA preferentially enriched integrated stress response and unfolded protein response genes, whereas SD showed a comparatively orthogonal, growth-permissive, mTOR-associated profile. Although IA-induced gene-expression suggests cellular stress, corticosterone measurements argued against systemic stress as the primary driver. These findings indicate that isoflurane recovery is neurophysiologically and molecularly distinct from restorative sleep.

papers.title: An acetylcholine-inhibited sleep-active hippocampal interneuron orchestrates memory consolidation.
papers.abstract: Memory reactivation during hippocampal ripples is critical for sleep-dependent memory consolidation. However, the molecular-to-circuit mechanism enabling sleep-predominant ripple generation remains unresolved. Here, we discovered that a sparse population of GABAergic interneurons in the mouse hippocampus specializes in gating ripple generation and memory consolidation. While all known genetically labeled hippocampal interneurons were highly active during wakefulness and rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep, genetic targeting of M2 acetylcholine receptor (Chrm2)-expressing neurons isolated a specific population preferentially active during non-REM (NREM) sleep and quiet wakefulness. These acetylcholine-inhibited interneurons inhibited the entire hippocampus in an infra-slow rhythm (∼0.015 Hz). Suppressing their activity in dorsal CA3 or ventral hippocampus impaired spatial and social memory, respectively. Furthermore, Chrm2+ neurons were closely associated with ripples; their activity bidirectionally modulated ripple occurrence via widespread inhibition. Thus, Chrm2+ interneurons are critical in linking neuromodulatory state to memory consolidation, offering genetically targeted access to sleep-active memory circuits implicated in cognitive disorders.

papers.title: Circadian and Sleep-Wake Modulation of EEG Functional Connectivity Across Brain States and Its Associations With Cognition in Humans.
papers.abstract: Sleep and circadian rhythms both influence human brain function, but their distinct contributions to large-scale network organization remain unclear. We quantified the effect of brain state (wake, NREM, REM), sleep-wake history, and circadian phase on functional connectivity using over 1,200 hours of artifact-free EEG recorded during a 10-day forced-desynchrony protocol. We derived principal components of functional connectivity and found that both sleep-wake history and circadian phase significantly modulated functional connectivity, with sleep-wake history exerting a broader influence. Complementary cosinor analyses further demonstrated circadian rhythmicity in several NREM and REM connectivity measures. Across sleep, global connectivity increased progressively during NREM sleep, particularly in the delta and sigma bands, but declined during REM sleep. During controlled resting wakefulness, increasing time awake was associated with higher global alpha-band connectivity, which was associated with poorer concurrent cognitive performance. Connectivity during NREM sleep was also associated with subsequent cognitive performance, with lower global theta and, to a lesser extent, higher sigma connectivity linked to better performance. REM connectivity was not associated with these cognitive measures. Together, these findings reveal opposing NREM and REM trajectories in large-scale EEG functional connectivity and show that these brain-state-specific network dynamics are shaped by both sleep-wake history and circadian phase and are associated with cognitive performance.

papers.title: REM Sleep Iota Oscillations Across the Lifespan
papers.abstract: Iota oscillations are a newly discovered marker of wakefulness and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. So far, iota in REM sleep has only been reported in the surface electroencephalography (EEG) of a small sample of young adults and in intracranial recordings of epileptic patients. Here, we investigated the presence of these oscillations in a large dataset (N=937) of high-density sleep EEG recordings from individuals 7 to 70 years old. We found that iota spectral peaks during REM sleep were between 25 and 40 Hz, slightly faster than in wake (25-35 Hz). Iota power was significantly associated with REM sleep architecture, increasing with both REM duration and across progressive sleep cycles. Iota peaks were observed in individuals of all ages, although the prevalence decreased gradually with age, from 88% in children to 44% in older adults. Most iota spectral peak properties (frequency, amplitude, timing, topography) likewise shifted with age. The most striking effect, however, was in bandwidth, such that children had narrow iota peaks, older adults had broad iota peaks, and 20-30 year olds could have either. It remains unclear whether narrowband and broadband iota are functionally equivalent. On shorter time scales (< 1 year), iota properties remained stable across measurements. Analyses of a separate dataset of monozygotic and dizygotic twins revealed high heritability of all iota peak properties except bandwidth. Overall, these results establish iota as a genetically determined trait-like marker of REM sleep with unique age-related changes. Iota oscillations open new avenues to investigate the interaction between sleep, genetics, development, and aging.

ai.reason: Large high-density EEG dataset characterizing REM spectral oscillations and architecture; relevant spectral/methodological background though focused on REM iota rather than NREM homeostasis.
ai.summary: Analyzed high-density sleep EEG from 937 individuals aged 7–70 and found that iota oscillations during REM sleep peak at 25–40 Hz, increase with REM duration and across sleep cycles, decline in prevalence from 88% in children to 44% in older adults, and show broadened bandwidth with age. Twin analyses indicated high heritability of most iota peak properties except bandwidth, supporting iota as a genetically determined, trait-like REM sleep marker.

papers.title: Layer 1 NDNF interneurons form distinct subpopulations with opposite activation patterns during sleep in freely behaving mice
papers.abstract: Non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep facilitates memory consolidation by transferring information from the hippocampus to the neocortex. This transfer is thought to occur primarily when hippocampal sharp-wave ripples (SWRs) and thalamocortical spindles are synchronized. However, the mechanisms underlying this synchronization remain unknown. In this study, we investigated the role of cortical layer 1 NDNF-expressing (L1 NDNF) interneurons in gating information transfer during SWR-spindle synchronization in NREM sleep. Using simultaneous cell-specific calcium imaging with a head-mounted microscope and local field potential recordings in freely moving mice, we compared the activity of L1 NDNF and L2/3 neurons across vigilance states and during NREM-specific oscillations. Our findings reveal that L1 NDNF neurons form three distinct populations, assembling into cell networks tuned to specific sleep stages. REM active L1 NDNF and L2/3 neurons exhibit opposite activation patterns during spindles. While L2/3 cells are mostly inactive during SWR, NREM, and REM active L1 NDNF cells inhibit the network upon SWR onset depending on their coupling with spindles. L1 NDNF neurons mediate slow inhibition primarily via GABAB receptors. Systemic application of a GABAB receptor antagonist resulted in decreased neuronal coupling of pyramidal cells but did not change the inhibitory responses during SWRs. Overall, these findings highlight the potential role of L1 NDNF neuron-mediated inhibition in the response to synchronized sleep oscillations, with potential implications for memory consolidation.

papers.title: Global Time-Aware Conditioning (GTC): A Mechanism for Time-Aware Pediatric Sleep Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Sleep physiology evolves throughout the night, with changes in sleep cycles, respiratory stability, and cardiovascular dynamics. However, self-supervised learning (SSL) methods for sleep typically process short, fixed-duration windows without explicitly modeling where each window occurs within the full sleep session. We introduce Global Time-Aware Conditioning (GTC), a mechanism that complements local positional encodings by conditioning latent representations on the global time-of-sleep of each input window. We integrate GTC into three representative SSL frameworks and evaluate them on five clinically relevant tasks with extreme class imbalance across two independent pediatric cohorts. GTC generally improves F1 and AUPRC across architectures and tasks, with gains persisting under cross-cohort transfer, highlighting the value of global temporal context for sleep representation learning.

papers.title: Behavioral, Transcriptomic, and Neuroinflammatory Effects of Sleep Deprivation: Insights From Separate Acute and Chronic Experimental Paradigms.
papers.abstract: Depression is a global health burden associated with sleep disruption and inflammation. While acute sleep deprivation (ASD) can alleviate depressive symptoms, chronic sleep deprivation (CSD) is a risk factor for mood disorders. However, the contrasting mechanisms underlying these opposing outcomes remain poorly understood. We integrated behavioral profiling, multi-region transcriptomics, and multiplex cytokine analysis to separately characterize the effects of ASD in a pain-depression comorbidity model and CSD in normal mice. Adult male C57BL/6J mice (n = 6 per group) were subjected to either a single 6-h total sleep deprivation (ASD) or 6-h daily sleep deprivation for 14 consecutive days (CSD). Behavioral testing included the tail suspension test (TST), open field test (OFT), elevated plus maze (EPM), and sucrose preference test (SPT). Following the interventions, five brain regions-prefrontal cortex (PFC), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), agranular insular cortex (AI), parietal cortex (PAR), and retrosplenial cortex (RSP)-were dissected. Cytokine levels were quantified using a multiplex panel targeting 15 analytes. Behavioral tests demonstrated that ASD alleviated despair-like behaviors induced by spared nerve injury surgery, whereas CSD resulted in anxiety- and despair-like behaviors. The prefrontal cortex (PFC) exhibited prominent transcriptomic responses to both ASD and CSD, with a substantial number of differentially expressed mRNAs. Transcriptome sequencing confirmed stable differential expression of mRNAs across multiple brain regions. Notable genes linked to depression, including Plin4 and Sult1a1, emerged as potential targets for further research. Ingenuity Pathway Analysis of differentially expressed mRNAs in the PFC indicated that IL-6 and TNF were primarily associated with these changes following ASD. Additionally, inflammatory factors such as BAFF, CHI3L1, IL-4, IL-6R alpha, IL-6, IL-10, TNFRSF1B, IL-12 p70, TWEAK, and osteopontin significantly decreased in the ASD group but increased in the CSD group. This study elucidates that ASD is associated with alleviation of despair-like behaviors and concurrent suppression of multiple inflammatory factors; however, the causal relationship between these observations requires further experimental validation. These findings open new research avenues for identifying potential depression treatment targets. Future research should explore the functional implications of these transcriptomic changes and their relevance for developing novel antidepressant strategies. papers.title: Effect of Long-Term Physical Exercise on Memory, Anxiety-Like Behavior, and Depression in Young and Aged Male Mice Subjected to Sleep Deprivation.
papers.abstract: This study evaluated whether chronic aerobic exercise could attenuate behavioral impairments associated with sleep deprivation (SD) in young and aged male mice. Young (3 months) and aged (18 months) Swiss mice were assigned to four groups: control, exercise (EXE), sleep deprivation (SD), and exercise followed by SD (EXE + SD). Animals performed treadmill training for 8 weeks and then underwent 72-hour SD. Behavioral tests assessed working memory (Y-maze), depression-like behavior (tail suspension), and anxiety-like behavior (elevated plus maze). The results suggest that age influences the effectiveness of exercise in mitigating sleep deprivation-induced behavioral deficits, opening avenues for future studies on the interaction between physical exercise, sleep, and aging.

papers.title: Phasic pupil responses to melanopsin- and cone-directed stimulation remain stable across circadian time
papers.abstract: Human pupil responses vary with time of day, but whether this reflects circadian modulation of specific photoreceptor pathways is unclear. Twelve healthy adults completed repeated pupillometry during a 40-hour ultra-short sleep-wake protocol that limited sustained wakefulness; data from eight met the quality-control criteria and were analysed. This design was intended to limit progressive accumulation of homeostatic sleep pressure across sampled circadian phase. During wake episodes, 0.4-Hz silent-substitution stimuli targeted broadband flux, melanopsin, luminance, L-M cone-opponent, or S-cone pathways. Salivary melatonin provided participant-specific period estimates. We separated slow tonic constriction from phasic pupil tracking and compared hierarchical circadian cosinor models with constant-level models. Constant-level models were favoured for phasic amplitude in all five conditions (log10 BF10 = -3.36 to -1.10). They were also favoured for tonic minimum in four conditions; L-M favoured the circadian model (log10 BF10 = 0.67), but the evidence was imprecise. Under the tested contrast, adaptation, and frequency, these data do not support circadian modulation of phasic photoreceptor-directed pupil tracking. Other metrics and smaller or non-sinusoidal effects remain possible.

papers.title: Sleep Spindles and Slow Oscillations as Potential Biomarkers and Therapeutic Targets in Mild-to-Moderate Alzheimer's Disease.
papers.abstract: This review critically evaluates evidence on sleep spindles (SP), slow oscillations (SOs), and their coordination in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease (AD), focusing on their relationships with cognition, AD biomarkers, and their therapeutic potential. Longitudinal studies associate greater SP and/or SO activity with better cognition and favourable amyloid and tau profiles after clinical onset. Spindle and SO coupling may index network integrity. Preserved NREM sleep oscillations are associated with lower orexin concentrations and weaker adverse relationships between orexin and cognitive and neuropsychiatric outcomes. Closed-loop acoustic stimulation and slow-oscillatory transcranial direct-current stimulation can modify SO activity, spindle activity, and coupling, although cognitive and biomarker benefits remain uncertain. Spindle-SO activity, including their temporal coupling, are associated with cognition and AD biomarkers across the disease continuum. Closed-loop acoustic and electrical stimulation can modify these oscillations, but biomarker-characterized trials in MCI and AD are needed to determine whether treatment produces durable cognitive and biomarker benefits.

papers.title: Sleep stage-specific heart rate variability feature-driven clustering analysis: identifying cardiac autonomic endotypes with long-term cardiovascular predictive value.
papers.abstract: Cardiovascular risk assessment in obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) has traditionally relied on the Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI). However, AHI primarily reflects respiratory event burden and may not adequately capture inter-individual heterogeneity in sleep-related cardiorespiratory regulation. This study aimed to identify sleep stage-specific heart rate variability (HRV) phenotypes and evaluate their associations with long-term cardiovascular outcomes. Data were obtained from the Sleep Heart Health Study (SHHS). After exclusion of participants with missing clinical covariates or outcome data, 4029 individuals were included. Linear and non-linear HRV features were extracted from stage-specific electrocardiographic segments during N2, N3, and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. K-means clustering was performed independently for each sleep stage after Z-score standardization, and the optimal cluster number was determined using silhouette coefficients and the elbow method. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models and Kaplan-Meier analyses were used to evaluate associations between HRV-informed phenotypes and all-cause mortality, coronary heart disease, and cardiovascular disease (CVD). Three HRV-informed phenotypes were identified within the selected clustering framework across N2, N3, and REM sleep stages: Stable (Cluster 0), Burden (Cluster 1), and High risk (Cluster 2). Compared with the Stable phenotype, the High-risk phenotype was consistently associated with increased cardiovascular risk, with the strongest association observed for incident CVD in the N2 stage [hazard ratio (HR) 1.468, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.280-1.684, P < 0.001]. Similar associations were observed in the N3 (HR 1.426, 95% CI 1.249-1.629, P < 0.001) and REM (HR 1.394, 95% CI 1.216-1.598, P < 0.001) stages. Sequential adjustment for AHI, oxygen desaturation index, arousal index, and sleep efficiency resulted in only minimal attenuation of hazard estimates, indicating that the prognostic associations were largely independent of conventional respiratory severity measures. In contrast, the Burden phenotype was consistently associated with lower all-cause mortality across all three sleep stages (HR 0.83-0.85, all P < 0.001). Subgroup analyses stratified by OSA severity demonstrated broadly consistent prognostic associations across AHI strata. Incorporating sleep stage-specific HRV features into conventional clinical phenotyping provides complementary prognostic information beyond traditional respiratory severity metrics. HRV-informed phenotyping may improve long-term cardiovascular risk stratification in patients with OSA.

papers.title: Sleep Stage Classification Across Heterogeneous EEG/EOG Channels with Multi-channel Differential Transformer.
papers.abstract: Classification of sleep stages is essential for assessing sleep quality and diagnosing sleep disorders. However, manual inspection of EEG characteristics for each stage is time-consuming and prone to human error. Although machine learning and deep learning methods have been actively developed, they continue to face challenges arising from the non-stationarity and variability of electroencephalography (EEG) and electrooculography (EOG) signals across diverse clinical configurations, often resulting in poor generalization. In this work, we propose SleepDIFFormer, a multi-channel differential transformer framework for heterogeneous EEG-EOG representation learning. SleepDIFFormer is trained across multiple sleep staging datasets, each treated as a source domain, with the goal of generalizing to unseen target domains. Specifically, it employs a Multi-channel Differential Transformer Architecture (MDTA) designed to process raw EEG and EOG signals while incorporating cross-domain alignment. Our approach mitigates spatial and temporal attention noise and learns a domain-invariant EEG-EOG representation through feature distribution alignment across datasets, thereby enhancing generalization to new domains. Empirically, we evaluated SleepDIFFormer on five diverse sleep staging datasets under domain generalization settings and benchmarked it against existing approaches, achieving superior performance. Furthermore, comprehensive ablation analyses and interpretation of the differential attention weights demonstrated their relevance to learning discriminative sleep EEG representations. These findings support the development of more generalizable approaches to automated sleep-stage classification. Our source code and checkpoint are made publicly available at https://github.com/Ben1001409/SleepDIFFormer.

papers.title: REM Atonia Index Cutoffs for REM Sleep Without Atonia: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis of Adult Diagnostic Performance.
papers.abstract: To synthesize evidence on REM Atonia Index (RAI) thresholds and reference values, quantify adult diagnostic performance for REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and distinguish diagnostic cutoffs from physiological reference limits and pediatric values. Methods: We conducted a focused systematic review of studies using automated RAI, rescreening studies from a previous review and updating PubMed/MEDLINE through July 27, 2026. Adult diagnostic accuracy was synthesized with a bivariate binomial-normal random-effects model. Continuous RAI differences were pooled as raw mean differences. Normative adult and pediatric evidence was synthesized separately because these represented different estimands. The review was retrospectively registered in OSF Registries on August 20, 2026 (https://osf.io/v3kqa). Thirty unique studies were included. Eight adult studies contributed to the diagnostic-accuracy meta-analysis; thresholds ranged from 0.80 to 0.90. Pooled sensitivity was 0.850 (95% CI, 0.766-0.908) and specificity 0.895 (95% CI, 0.814-0.944). Eight studies contributed continuous data; RAI was lower in RBD by a pooled mean difference of -0.263 (95% CI, -0.335 to -0.190). Only two methodologically non-equivalent adult studies provided physiological reference limits, 0.85 and 0.91, precluding pooling. Pediatric evidence supported age-conditioned interpretation. Adult chin-EMG RAI shows good overall discrimination of established RBD, but current evidence does not support a universal numerical boundary for REM sleep without atonia. Evidence defining physiological reference limits is substantially less developed than diagnostic evidence, and normal RAI varies with age. RAI should therefore be reported continuously, with thresholds interpreted according to their intended diagnostic or physiological purpose.

papers.title: Sleep Duration and Mental Well-Being Among Older Chinese Adults: A Four-Wave Fixed-Effects Analysis Using CHARLS.
papers.abstract: To examine within-person associations between nighttime sleep duration and mental well-being among older Chinese adults. We analyzed four waves of the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS; 2011-2018) using individual fixed-effects linear regressions with wave fixed effects and individual-clustered standard errors. Outcomes were CES-D-10 depressive symptoms and reverse-coded life satisfaction. Sleep was modeled continuously and categorically, with main categories of ≤6 h, >6 to <9 h, and ≥9 h; sensitivity models used ≤ 5 h, >5 to <9 h, and ≥9 h. Among observations with valid CES-D-10 data, 36.74% met the ≥10 screening threshold. Each additional hour of sleep was associated with lower CES-D-10 scores (β = -0.305) and higher life satisfaction (β = 0.015). Compared with the main reference range, short sleep was associated with higher CES-D-10 scores (β = 0.846) and lower life satisfaction (β = -0.046). Long-sleep estimates varied by specification and outcome. Shorter nighttime sleep duration, particularly sleep in the operational short-sleep category, was associated with poorer mental well-being within individuals over time. Usual sleep duration can inform mood and sleep assessment but should not substitute for evaluation of sleep quality or sleep disorders.

papers.title: Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome: Unloading the Respiratory System with Expiratory Pressure.
papers.abstract: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS) is traditionally interpreted through the lens of coexistent obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), yet the mechanisms by which continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) improves daytime hypercapnia without providing ventilatory support remain incompletely explained. This Perspective proposes that abdominal obesity-induced depletion of expiratory reserve volume (ERV) and functional residual capacity (FRC), with consequent reduction in end-expiratory lung volume (EELV), may represent upstream mechanical abnormalities linking OSA, increased work of breathing, sleep hypoventilation, and daytime hypercapnia. Reduced EELV worsens pharyngeal collapsibility by decreasing caudal traction, while simultaneously shifting tidal volume toward a mechanically inefficient portion of the respiratory system curve, characterized by impaired compliance, and increased elastic, resistive respiratory work and possibly threshold loading. Within this framework, OHS emerges when respiratory burden (the mechanical load on the pulmonary apparatus due to excess weight) exceeds ventilatory reserve (an ensemble of respiratory drive and its modifiers such as sleep-state control, leptin signaling, and genetic factors). CPAP and expiratory PAP may provide, in addition to upper-airway splinting, a mechanical unloading by raising EELV, improving respiratory mechanics, and reducing the pressure cost of ventilation. In this context, weight loss represents the ultimate structural unloading therapy, whereas pressure support may be required when unloading alone is insufficient to restore adequate ventilation. Future studies should measure ERV, FRC/EELV, respiratory effort, and mechanics to better phenotype OHS, and understand whether optimizing expiratory pressure before adding ventilatory support actually improves ventilation.

papers.title: Nonlinear Feature Modeling Using Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks in Electroencephalography for Depression Classification: Deep Learning Study.
papers.abstract: Depression is a common mental disorder that seriously affects mental health and quality of life. Traditional depression diagnosis mainly relies on clinical interviews and subjective assessments, which may lead to variability in diagnostic outcomes. Electroencephalogram (EEG)-based computer-aided diagnosis has emerged as a promising, objective approach for depression recognition. However, effectively modeling the complex nonlinear characteristics of EEG signals remains a major challenge for existing deep learning methods. This study aimed to investigate the applicability of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) for EEG-based depression recognition and to evaluate the effectiveness of KAN-based nonlinear modeling frameworks on frequency-domain EEG features. KAN was introduced into EEG-based depression recognition to enhance nonlinear feature representation of brain electrical signals. Two representative KAN-based convolutional architectures, ConvKAN and its efficiency-optimized variant ConvKAN Efficient, were systematically investigated for EEG classification tasks. These architectures incorporated KANLinear layers together with dynamic grid updating, enhanced weight initialization, and regularization strategies to improve nonlinear modeling capability while maintaining computational efficiency. Extensive experiments were conducted on the EDRA dataset, and the proposed framework was compared with conventional convolutional neural network-based methods and traditional machine learning approaches. Model performance was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score metrics. Experimental results demonstrated that the KAN-based frameworks achieved superior EEG classification performance compared with conventional convolutional neural network-based methods and traditional machine learning approaches. Among the evaluated models, ConvKAN Efficient achieved the best overall performance, with accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score all exceeding 94% on the EDRA dataset. The results indicate that KAN-based architectures can effectively capture the complex nonlinear characteristics of EEG signals while preserving high computational efficiency. This study systematically demonstrates the applicability of KAN-based nonlinear modeling frameworks to EEG-based depression recognition. The proposed framework provides a scalable and effective approach for EEG signal analysis and offers valuable technical support for both theoretical research and clinical applications in computer-aided depression recognition.

papers.title: Beyond the pump: a narrative review of the acute molecular, metabolic, and neuropsychological responses to a bout of resistance exercise.
papers.abstract: Resistance training is widely recognized for its chronic adaptations, including strength, muscle hypertrophy, and improvements in musculoskeletal health. However, a single bout of resistance exercise also elicits a range of acute physiological and psychological responses across multiple systems. These immediate responses have generally been examined within individual physiological domains, with less attention given to their coexistence and temporal overlap following a single session. This narrative review synthesizes evidence relating to the acute systemic effects of a single bout of resistance exercise. Literature was identified through iterative searches of electronic databases and reference lists, with emphasis on primary human studies directly examining acute responses, alongside relevant systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and mechanistic literature. Acute resistance exercise induces responses across endocrine and myokine, metabolic, vascular, pain-related, psychological, cognitive, and sleep-related domains. Contracting skeletal muscle releases myokines and other signalling molecules with potential systemic actions. Post-exercise energy expenditure and muscle protein synthesis may remain elevated during recovery, while glucose uptake and insulin sensitivity are enhanced. Acute resistance exercise can also produce exercise-induced hypoalgesia, reduce state anxiety, improve aspects of executive function and cognitive performance, and may influence sleep continuity and neurophysiological activity. These responses differ in their evidential basis and physiological significance, encompassing directly observed short-term effects, proposed regulatory mechanisms, and more tentative hypotheses regarding longer-term implications. A single bout of resistance exercise produces temporally overlapping responses across multiple physiological and psychological systems. These responses should not be assumed to represent adaptive remodelling or direct mechanisms of chronic health benefit. Nevertheless, integrating them provides a broader perspective on the immediate multisystem consequences of resistance exercise and may help inform future research examining how repeated acute responses relate to longer-term adaptation and health outcomes.

papers.title: Single-Lead EEG-based virtual reality motion sickness detection using interpretable feature selection.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a key method for detecting virtual reality motion sickness (VRMS), but multi-lead recordings and high-dimensional features increase processing complexity, device cost, and user burden. This study proposes a SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based single-lead modeling and feature-screening framework to reduce the number of EEG leads and feature dimensions for lightweight VRMS detection. Six classical deep-learning EEG decoding models were used to assess the contribution of each lead via SHAP values and identify the optimal single lead. Handcrafted features were then extracted and selected using a correlation-SHAP strategy, and XGBoost was adopted for final classification. FT11 showed competitive and relatively consistent performance across the evaluated models and was selected as the target lead after integrating SHAP-based lead importance, single-lead classification performance, frequency-band differences, and physiological relevance. Under the window-level tenfold cross-validation protocol used in this study, the proposed model achieved an accuracy of 87.53% ± 0.73% using seven selected features, which was 9.55 percentage points lower than the full-lead full-feature model and 0.69 percentage points lower than the single-lead full-feature model. These findings demonstrate an interpretable framework for identifying a compact single-lead and feature configuration for VRMS-related EEG discrimination. An additional post hoc LOSO test of the globally selected configuration showed limited performance on held-out participants. Because the lead, classifier, and feature configuration had been selected globally before LOSO testing, these results should not be interpreted as a fully independent estimate of cross-subject generalization.

papers.title: Considering counterfactual prediction models in sleep research: A demonstration of incident stroke prediction in an observational cohort study.
papers.abstract: Data-driven risk prediction algorithms are increasingly common. However, studies suggesting that a single set of variables are most "important" within a given risk prediction model ignore the reality that other equally useful models containing entirely different features may exist. We aim to use a novel approach (Model Path Selection) to demonstrate that, for any given health outcome, there are likely many comparable counterfactual models including different sets of variables. We focus on incident stroke as a scientifically meaningful outcome to motivate this demonstration. Model Path Selection uses an iterative model-building procedure to illustrate a set of counterfactual prediction models ("paths"). We applied Model Path Selection to Sleep Heart Health Study data (N = 4,512 adults) to predict 5-year incident stroke, considering 30 features comprising demographics, self-reported and measured medical risk factors, polysomnography, and self-reported sleep. Area Under the Curve was estimated for each resulting path based on 10-fold cross-validation. Model Path Selection identified 61 unique counterfactual models. 13 of these achieved Area Under the Curves between 0.81 and 0.82. Area Under the Curves of the remaining models ranged from 0.53 to 0.68 (median 0.61). All 13 top models included age plus various combinations of other features (polysomnography indices, body mass index, and/or the Short Form 36 mental and physical component scores). Model Path Selection can illuminate counterfactual prediction models, differentiate features that may be uniquely predictive from those that can be swapped out with other features, enhance reproducibility, inform the design of clinically practical predictive tools, and suggest sleep-related risk factors to be targeted for health promotion.

papers.title: Heart rate rises most during REM sleep after semaglutide initiation: a matched longitudinal cohort study
papers.abstract: Study Objectives: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists raise resting heart rate. We asked whether, after semaglutide initiation, the increase is larger during rapid eye movement (REM) sleep than during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep. Methods: In the Human Phenotype Project, an Israeli cohort of generally healthy adults aged 40 to 70 years, 96 of 494 self-reported semaglutide initiators had a home sleep study (WatchPAT; sleep stages estimated from peripheral arterial tone and actigraphy) before and at least three months after starting. Each was propensity-matched 1:1 to a never-user of GLP-1 drugs measured at the same visits. We estimated the initiators' change minus their controls' change (difference-in-differences). The REM minus NREM contrast was designated primary after an exploratory analysis. Results: Relative to controls (90 to 94 pairs), heart rate rose during nocturnal wake (+3.89 beats per minute [bpm], 95% confidence interval 2.35 to 5.44), NREM sleep (+4.82 bpm, 3.12 to 6.52) and REM sleep (+6.25 bpm, 4.42 to 7.91); the REM increase exceeded the NREM increase by 1.42 bpm (0.98 to 1.89). The excess persisted across matching designs and on a relative scale; the proportion of REM sleep did not change. Never-users with similar weight loss showed no REM sleep heart-rate rise (+0.40 bpm, -0.63 to 1.50). Heart-rate variability decreases disappeared after adjustment for heart rate. Conclusions: Semaglutide initiation was associated with higher heart rate throughout sleep, most during REM sleep, unexplained by weight loss. Clinic measurements may understate this effect. Confirmation with polysomnographic staging is needed.

papers.title: Integrated Transcriptomic and Single-Cell Sequencing Identifies Altered Expression of Circadian Rhythm-Related Genes Pomc and Bmp4 in Post-Stroke Depression.
papers.abstract: Post-stroke depression (PSD) is a serious complication that significantly hinders stroke patients' recovery and quality of life. Uncovering the molecular changes that drive PSD is vital for understanding how depression develops following a stroke. In this study, we established a reproducible PSD model using minimally invasive photochemical-induced focal cortical lesion. Transcriptomic sequencing demonstrated that dysregulation of circadian entrainment genes is a central pathway in the development of post-stroke depressive-like behaviors. Protein-protein interaction network analysis of these circadian rhythm-related genes identified six hub genes. Four of these, including Pomc and Bmp4, exhibited expression patterns consistent with experimental validation. Integrated single-cell transcriptomic analysis further pinpointed cell-type-specific expression abnormalities of Pomc in endothelial cells and Bmp4 in oligodendrocytes. Subsequently, in silico perturbation analysis further indicated that their shared underlying regulatory mechanisms involve cell adhesion and extracellular matrix interaction. Collectively, using transcriptomic and single-cell sequencing in a PSD model, this study revealed altered expression patterns of circadian rhythm-related genes, providing potential targets for further investigation into the pathogenesis of PSD.

papers.title: Amplitude-integrated electroencephalogram (aEEG): A bedside window into newborn brain function in the NICU.
papers.abstract: Amplitude-integrated electroencephalography (aEEG) remains an important tool for bedside neonatal brain monitoring. papers.title: [Neurocognitive characteristics in children with sluggish cognitive tempo].
papers.abstract: The aim of this study was to assess the neurocognitive characteristics of children diagnosed with sluggish cognitive tempo (SCT) and to evaluate the efficacy of Cortexin in addressing this condition. The main study group included 40 children aged 12 to 14 years with symptoms consistent with SCT manifestations. The comparison group consisted of 30 children with combined ADHD (ADHD-C), also aged 12 to 14 years. The control group comprised 30 children in the same age range without any neuropsychiatric disorders. The study used several methods, including S. Lee's SCT scale for assessing the severity of SCT symptoms, the Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory (MFI-20), the Daytime Sleepiness Scale, and T.A. Fotekova and T.V. Akhutina's reading skills assessment method, the «Working Memory» method to quantifying working memory capabilities, the TOVA computer test, and EEG (routine and spectral analysis). Cortexin was administered intramuscularly at a standard dosage of 10 mg every other day across 10 injections to patients diagnosed with SCT. The study results showed that children with SCT, in comparison to their counterparts with ADHD-C and healthy peers, exhibited significantly more pronounced asthenic symptoms and a higher prevalence of comorbid learning disorders. Quantitative EEG analysis revealed a reduced theta-to-alpha wave power ratio in the anterior cerebral cortex of the SCT group compared with the ADHD cohort. These findings support the hypothesis that children with SCT are less prone to exhibiting deficits in inhibition processes, while instead demonstrating a decline in overall levels of functional activity maintenance. A follow-up assessment after treatment revealed improvements in inattention, severity of working memory impairment, asthenic symptoms, and reading skills in 82% of cases. Additionally, EEG analysis post-treatment indicated a reduction in alpha-band power in the frontal and central leads of both hemispheres, suggesting enhanced overall cortical activation. This study has delineated several cognitive characteristics associated with SCT in children and demonstrated that administering Cortexin significantly alleviates the primary symptoms of SCT and mitigates the manifestation of major comorbid disorders.

papers.title: Modification of locomotion-respiration coupling in patients with obstructive sleep apnea syndrome.
papers.abstract: Locomotion is a complex motor task integrating sensory-motor and cognitive inputs through central pattern generator control. Locomotion-respiration coupling (LRC), defined as the synchronization between gait and breathing events, has been described during running and walking. Patients with obstructive sleep apnea syndrome (OSAS) exhibit altered gait patterns during wakefulness, which appear to be partially independent of nocturnal symptomatic treatment. While intermittent hypoxia may induce long-term ("fixed") central nervous system alterations, OSAS patients also display "reversible" adaptive mechanisms during wakefulness aimed at preventing upper airway (UA) collapse, involving changes in respiratory control and posture. Whether these adaptive mechanisms affect LRC and contribute to gait alterations remains unknown. Ten awake patients with controlled OSAS treated with a mandibular advancement device (MAD) and ten matched healthy controls performed a one-minute walking trial on an instrumented treadmill with motion capture. Ventilation was assessed via thoracic expansion, and spatiotemporal gait parameters were extracted from kinematic and force platform data. LRC was quantified using phase-locking values (PLV) between ventilatory events and sagittal-plane joint kinematics. OSAS patients were assessed both with and without their MAD. Compared with controls, OSAS patients exhibited a longer double-stance phase and a shorter swing phase. Expiratory events occurred preferentially during double stance in OSAS patients, whereas controls showed a higher occurrence during swing. PLV analysis revealed increased synchronization between inspiratory events and hip and knee motion, as well as between expiratory events and trunk and hip motion in OSAS patients. These significative differences were no longer observed when patients wore their MAD. Logistic regression demonstrated that PLV metrics of inspiratory-hip and expiratory-trunk coupling effectively discriminated OSAS patients from controls, but not when UA stabilization was applied. Awake patients with controlled OSAS exhibit altered gait patterns characterized by increased locomotion-respiration coupling. This heightened synchronization likely reflects adaptive, reversible strategies aimed at limiting UA collapsibility during wakefulness rather than fixed hypoxia-related impairments alone. LRC may represent a functional marker of daytime motor alterations in OSAS and a potential target for interventions addressing UA mechanics beyond nocturnal treatment.

papers.title: [Spectral-topographic features of EEG in patients with varying rates of alcohol dependence progression].
papers.abstract: To compare the spectral-topographic characteristics of the background electroencephalogram (EEG) in patients with alcohol dependence, differing in disease progression rate, as part of a pilot study. A total of 40 male patients with a confirmed diagnosis of alcohol dependence (F10.2 according to ICD-10) were examined. Utilizing a retrospective evaluation of the development of alcohol withdrawal syndrome (AWS), participants were classified into two distinct groups: those exhibiting rapid progression (≤3 years, n=23) and those with slow progression (≥12 years, n=17). Background EEG recordings were obtained using a 16-channel system (10-20 configuration), followed by spectral analysis of absolute power in the theta, alpha-1, alpha-2, beta-1, and beta-2 frequency bands. The results indicate the presence of a distinct neurophysiological endophenotype associated with the rapid progression of alcohol dependence. Key characteristics of this endophenotype include a overall decrease in the power of the alpha-1 rhythm, particularly in the front-central leads; a decline in theta power (excluding the parietal region); a frontal-specific reduction in beta-1 power; and a significant prevalence of low-amplitude EEG patterns.

papers.title: Effects of EEG neurofeedback in adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a systematic review of randomised and non-randomised studies.
papers.abstract: Pharmacotherapy is recommended as the first-line treatment for adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), yet some individuals show partial or inadequate response associated with adverse effects. These limitations have prompted interest in adjunctive or alternative interventions. Electroencephalography (EEG) neurofeedback is a non-pharmacological intervention for ADHD, which enables self-regulation of neural activity. This systematic review synthesised clinical, cognitive, and electrophysiological outcomes of EEG neurofeedback in adult ADHD, and examined standard versus personalised training protocols. Following PRISMA guidelines, four databases (PubMed, ScienceDirect, Ovid, Web of Science) were searched from 1960 to October 2025 for this PROSPERO-registered review (ID: CRD420251020898). Eligible studies included adults (≥ 18 years) with a formal ADHD diagnosis undergoing EEG neurofeedback. Outcomes comprised symptom severity, cognitive performance, electrophysiology, and adverse events. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 and ROBINS-I V2. Seven studies (three RCTs, four non-randomised; n = 390) met inclusion criteria. Protocols included theta/beta (n = 1), slow cortical potential (n = 1), alpha downregulation training (n = 1) and personalised approaches guided by individual alpha peak frequency (n = 3) or QEEG profiles (n = 1). Naturalistic and personalised studies reported large symptom reductions, whereas RCTs revealed small, generally non-significant effects relative to controls. Cognitive improvements were inconsistently reported and largely attributable to practice effects. Electrophysiological changes were protocol-specific without convergence across studies. No treatment-related adverse events were observed. Evidence remains limited by methodological heterogeneity, small samples, variable controls, inconsistent learning metrics, and risk of bias. papers.title: Quantitative Analysis of Electroencephalography in Hypnosis: A Neurophysiological Approach.
papers.abstract: Hypnosis is a unique state of consciousness marked by heightened response to suggestions, focused attention, and altered cognitive control. This article explores the neural connections involved in hypnosis through electroencephalography (EEG) studies, examining brain changes during hypnosis and their relationship to hypnotic depth and susceptibility. Theta waves, linked to hypnotic depth, are stronger in highly hypnotizable individuals, while gamma waves are associated with focus, suggestion acceptance, and emotional responses. Hypnosis also induces frequency-dependent reorganization of large-scale brain connectivity, particularly in frontal-parietal and attentional networks, enhancing subjective experiences and responsiveness. EEG patterns reveal more dynamic neural activity during hypnosis, which cannot be captured by linear metrics alone. Hemispheric analysis shows greater left-hemisphere activity in highly hypnotizable individuals, particularly in emotionally and verbally mediated tasks, challenging the right-hemisphere dominance model. Event related potential (ERP) findings show that hypnosis affects information processing at both pre-attentional and cognitive levels. These insights contribute to understanding hypnosis' impact on the brain and its potential for personalized therapeutic interventions.

Multivariable logistic regression was used to examine the associations between sleep trajectories and incident CRMM ascertained between 2018 and 2020. Subgroup analyses and sensitivity analyses were further conducted to validate the robustness of the findings. Three sleep duration trajectory patterns were identified: normal-stable (33.9% of the cohort), normal-fluctuating decline (52.0%), and short-rapid decline (14.1%). During a median follow-up of 2 years, the primary outcome (incident CRMM) occurred in 108 participants (3.8%). Compared with normal-stable group, those in normal-fluctuating decline and short-rapid decline groups had an increased risk of CRMM (ORs of 2.30 [95%CI, 1.35-3.91] and 3.75 [95%CI, 1.99-7.07], respectively) after adjustment for multiple covariates. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of these associations, which were independent of key baseline characteristics and missing data. In postmenopausal women, short and declining sleep duration trajectories are strong, independent risk factors for CRMM. Public health and clinical interventions should prioritize maintaining stable, adequate sleep to mitigate multimorbidity risk in this population.

A total of 65 subjects participated in the study, comprising 40 males (61.5%) and 25 females (38.5%), with a mean age of 52.86±9.75 years. The subjects were categorized into two distinct groups: the main group, consisting of 37 patients with OSA and an apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) of more than 15 episodes per hour, and the control group, consisting of 28 subjects without OSA and an AHI of less than 5 episodes per hour. The diagnostic procedure for all subjects encompassed anthropometric measurements, polysomnography, and ultrasound imaging of the brachiocephalic arteries (BCA). The assessment of chronic cerebral ischemia (CCI) and hypertension (HTN) was conducted. IL-2 and IL-4 levels were measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Among patients diagnosed with OSA, CCI was detected in 75.7% of cases, and atherosclerotic changes in the BCA were observed in 89.2%. Furthermore, these patients presented with a bilateral increase in the diameters of the common carotid artery (CCA) and the internal carotid artery (ICA) (p<0.05), alongside a noted increase in IL-2 levels and a significantly reduced IL-4 levels. In the main group, a positive correlation was established between the diameter of the left ICA and IL-4 (r=0.421, p=0.009), as well as between the diameter of the right ICA and IL-4 (r=0.482, p=0.003). A positive association was also observed between the detected atherosclerotic alterations and neck circumference (r=0.269, p=0.030), AHI (r=0.255, p=0.041), HTN (r=0.336, p=0.006), and CCI (r=0.255, p=0.041). The findings of this study demonstrate that patients with OSA exhibit increasingly persistent and significant abnormalities in the extracranial arteries as the pathological process advances. The noted dilation of the ICA and the CCA in the main group is likely due to vascular remodeling and reduced IL-4 levels. The established correlation between atherosclerotic changes in the BCA and metrics such as neck circumference, AHI, HTN, and CCI suggests that OSA may directly induce pathological processes in vascular walls, thereby contributing to the emergence of comorbid conditions. The absence of a definitive link between BCA atherosclerosis and IL-4 levels in OSA patients may be attributable to the relatively small sample size, warranting further research.

papers.title: [Experience in the implementation of a comprehensive non-pharmacological therapeutic program at the Center for Cognitive and Psycho-Emotional Health].
papers.abstract: To analyze the outcomes of a complex non-pharmacological treatment regimen administered to patients at the daytime hospital (DH) of the Center for Cognitive and Psycho-Emotional Health (CCPH) and to evaluate the changes in the cognitive and psycho-emotional state of the patients. The study included 103 patients attending the CCPH DH, with a mean age of 46.98±14.32 years; 76.7% were female. Participants were categorized into three distinct groups: Group 1 with predominantly cognitive impairments (CIs), Group 2 with predominantly psycho-emotional disorders, and Group 3 with sleep disorders. Cognitive and psycho-emotional statuses were assessed using widely accepted tests and assessment scales. Each participant underwent a tailored five-day course of non-pharmacological therapy, which integrated cognitive training, biofeedback-based electroencephalography training, physical therapy, and neurostimulation techniques. Treatment outcomes were assessed after the intervention. Following the therapeutic intervention, 91.26% of participants demonstrated clinical improvement, with the greatest improvement observed in Group 2 (96.6%). No deterioration in clinical status was noted among any of the patients, thereby affirming the safety of the therapeutic interventions. Neuropsychological test results indicated a statistically significant improvement across all three groups (p<0.05), reflected in enhanced cognitive metrics and a reduction in anxiety and depressive symptoms among patients with pre-dementia CIs, anxiety disorders, and chronic insomnia. While a tendency towards improvement was noted in patients with severe ICs, the changes did not reach statistical significance, particularly in patients with isolated depressive disorders, potentially due to the limited sample size. Moreover, patients within Group 3 showed improvements in sleep during the therapy. The findings suggest that a five-day non-pharmacological intervention with an integrated approach represents an effective and safe method for the maintenance and enhancement of cognitive and psycho-emotional health.

papers.title: Enhancement of gut-microbiome-based classification of prodromal Parkinson's Disease cases by hyperparameter tuning, integration of multimodal data, and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's Disease (PD) is often preceded by a prodromal phase marked by non-motor symptoms such as REM Sleep Behaviour Disorder (RBD), gastrointestinal dysfunction, and olfactory impairment. Mounting evidence implicates gut microbiota in the early pathophysiology of PD. In this study, we aimed to enhance the classification of prodromal PD using gut microbiota profiles, with a focus on model performance and biomarker identification. Publicly available gut microbiome datasets of individuals with RBD and healthy controls were analyzed. Following batch correction and genus-level filtering, we identified six taxa significantly depleted in both RBD and PD groups, all belonging to short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing genera. Hyperparameter tuning on the testing set achieved an AUC of 0.889. When combining microbial and clinical features, the model achieved a peak mean AUC of 0.917. Feature selection identified 11 top-ranked features, yielding an AUC of 0.849. Using only the six differentially abundant SCFA-producing taxa, the model retained a strong predictive capacity with a mean AUC of 0.853. These results demonstrate the utility of gut microbiota, particularly SCFA-producing taxa, in the early identification of prodromal PD. Integration with select clinical features further improves model performance, supporting their potential role in early diagnostic frameworks.

papers.title: Voluntary wheel running selectively preserves skeletal muscle during pancreatic cancer cachexia despite persistent systemic alterations
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is frequently associated with cancer cachexia, involving alterations across multiple physiological systems. Whether distinct exercise paradigms similarly influence these compartments remains unclear. We compared voluntary wheel running (VWR) and treadmill running (TR) using an integrative physiological approach in a murine model of pancreatic cancer cachexia. Methods Male C57BL/6J mice bearing UN-KC-6141 pancreatic tumor cells were allocated to inactive control (CaCTL), VWR or TR groups and compared with healthy controls. Tumor progression, body composition, skeletal muscle, adipose tissue, hepatic metabolism, systemic inflammation, energy expenditure and behavior were assessed. Analysis of covariance determined whether tissue-mass differences remained evident after adjustment for tumor burden. Results UN-KC-6141 tumors induced a systemic cachectic phenotype involving skeletal muscle and adipose tissue wasting, hepatic metabolic remodeling, systemic inflammation and behavioral alterations. VWR slowed tumor growth, reduced final tumor mass, improved the body-weight trajectory and preserved lean and skeletal muscle mass, whereas TR did not reproduce these adaptations. Greater gastrocnemius mass with VWR remained evident after adjustment for tumor mass, indicating that reduced tumor burden alone was insufficient to account for muscle preservation. In contrast, adipose tissue wasting, hepatic metabolic remodeling and systemic inflammation remained largely unaffected. TR was also associated with a less favorable body-weight trajectory and greater fat mass loss than in inactive tumor-bearing mice. Exploratory metabolic phenotyping revealed distinct feeding, sleep and resting energy expenditure patterns between the two exercise paradigms. Conclusions VWR selectively preserved skeletal muscle within a persistently altered systemic environment, whereas the TR protocol used here did not reproduce these adaptations. These findings reveal tissue-specific exercise responsiveness during pancreatic cancer cachexia and highlight exercise paradigm characteristics as determinants of tumor-host adaptation.

papers.title: An incidental heterozygous ATP7B nonsense variant leading to a diagnostic pitfall for Wilson disease: a pediatric case report.
papers.abstract: Wilson disease (WD) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by pathogenic variants in ATP7B, resulting in impaired copper transport and progressive copper accumulation, most prominently affecting the liver. With the growing use of genetic testing, incidental detection of ATP7B pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants in individuals without typical hepatic phenotypes can prompt overdiagnosis and unnecessary investigations. This case highlights the importance of interpreting a single heterozygous ATP7B variant in the context of phenotype and a standardized biochemical diagnostic pathway for WD. A 13-year-old Han Chinese boy presented with recurrent brief paroxysmal attacks for > 1 year, markedly worsened over the preceding month. Episodes were triggered by rising from sitting, characterized by transient postural instability with unilateral head deviation and ipsilateral dystonic/choreiform movements, lasted ~ 10 s, and resolved spontaneously. Consciousness was preserved, with no incontinence, convulsions, or postictal symptoms. Interictal neurological examination was normal. Ambulatory EEG monitoring captured three typical attacks without epileptiform discharges or ictal EEG correlates, and brain MRI was unremarkable. A slit-lamp examination revealed no Kayser-Fleischer ring. A low serum copper level (9.43 µmol/L; reference 10.50-29.90) prompted further evaluation; genetic testing incidentally identified a heterozygous ATP7B variant (NM_000053.4:c.2851 C > T; p.Gln951Ter), reported as likely pathogenic. WD was considered. However, ceruloplasmin was normal (231.6 mg/L; reference 200.0-420.0 mg/L), ceruloplasmin oxidase activity measured by the p-phenylenediamine method was normal (0.372 OD; reference > 0.200 OD), liver biochemistry was normal (ALT 11 U/L, AST 16 U/L, GGT 14 U/L; bilirubin within reference range), and abdominal ultrasound showed a normal liver and biliary tree. Crucially, a follow-up quantitative 24-hour urinary copper test was strictly normal, and parental segregation analysis confirmed that the ATP7B variant represented a paternally inherited heterozygous state without biochemical evidence of Wilson disease, making active Wilson disease highly unlikely. This case illustrates a critical diagnostic pitfall: incidental heterozygous ATP7B variants can trigger severe diagnostic anchoring bias. To prevent overdiagnosis, genetic findings must be subordinated to strict phenotype-driven evaluations, formal Leipzig scoring, and definitive biochemical gold standards.

papers.title: Early Postoperative Psychological Resilience Patterns and Associated Factors in Patients with Knee Stiffness Undergoing Arthroscopic Release Surgery: A Latent Class Growth Model Study.
papers.abstract: Knee stiffness substantially impairs mobility and quality of life. Although arthroscopic release can improve joint function, little is known about early postoperative changes in psychological resilience among these patients. This study aimed to identify heterogeneous early postoperative psychological resilience patterns in patients with knee stiffness undergoing arthroscopic release surgery and to explore factors associated with pattern membership. A prospective observational study was conducted among patients undergoing arthroscopic release for knee stiffness. Psychological resilience was assessed using the Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale at four time points: admission before surgery, 3 days after surgery, 2 weeks after surgery, and 1 month after surgery. Latent class growth modeling was used to identify early postoperative resilience pattern groups. Univariate analyses and multinomial logistic regression were conducted to explore factors associated with pattern membership. Multicollinearity among candidate predictors was assessed before multivariable modeling. A total of 240 patients completed all four assessments. The LCGM identified three early postoperative psychological resilience pattern groups: the Low Resilience Declining Group (17.1%), the Moderate Resilience Stable Group (68.8%), and the High Resilience Increasing Group (14.2%). Multinomial logistic regression using standardized continuous psychosocial predictors showed that, compared with the High Resilience Increasing Group, patients in the Low Resilience Declining Group had lower perceived social support and poorer sleep quality. Compared with the High Resilience Increasing Group, patients in the Moderate Resilience Stable Group were more likely to have a primary-school education or below, lower perceived social support, and lower ERRI scores. Psychological resilience showed heterogeneous patterns during the early postoperative period after arthroscopic release for knee stiffness. The findings may help identify patients who are psychologically vulnerable during early recovery, but should be interpreted as exploratory because of the single-center design, short follow-up duration, and limited subgroup sizes. Further multicenter studies with longer follow-up and orthopedic outcome measures are needed to validate these early postoperative patterns and clarify their clinical significance.
